one_liner: Rust/C AVX-512 static search tree for sorted u32/u64 keys; about 10% faster lookups than STX B-Tree in SOSD.
what_it_does: A static, in-memory index over sorted u64 or u32 keys, each paired with a value of the same integer type (in SOSD, the key's position in the data array), built once from two parallel arrays via Rust FAST::new(keys, values) or the C ABI create_fast64/create_fast32. A lookup returns the pair of values that bracket the query (the value of the largest key <= query and the value of the next key), which the caller uses as a search bound over the underlying sorted array. It is not a map: there are no inserts, deletes or iteration, and no found/not-found result.
how_it_is_fast: Named after Kim et al.'s FAST (Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, SIGMOD 2010), the code builds a pointer-free B+-tree bottom-up in which every node is a 128-byte-aligned page: one 64-byte cache line of keys (8 u64 or 16 u32), then one line of child offsets, or of values at the leaves. Each level does a branch-free node search in C (one AVX-512 broadcast, one unsigned compare-to-mask and one popcount), and the count indexes straight into the offset line, so a lookup reads one page per level with fanout 8 for u64 keys or 16 for u32. The SOSD authors credit its multithreaded scaling to few cache misses and to AVX-512 overlapping compute with memory reads.
when_to_use: Read-only, build-once lower-bound lookups over sorted, unique u64 or u32 integer keys where the value is an array position, for example a sparse index over a large sorted array followed by a last-mile binary search.
x86-64 servers with AVX-512F, like the paper's Xeon Gold 6230, where you build and run on the same CPU model.

Throughput-bound lookups across many threads. SOSD measured the highest relative scaling of any structure: 32x its single-thread throughput at 40 threads. Its latency barely changed with a memory fence between lookups.
32-bit keys. Each 512-bit compare covers 16 keys, and SOSD notes that tree structures gain from 32-bit keys while learned indexes do not.
As a reproducible SIMD-tree baseline in index research, since it is the exact code behind SOSD's FAST numbers (SOSD pins its final commit, b3d15a9).
when_not_to_use: Any workload with updates. There is no insert or delete, so every change means a full rebuild, and SOSD found FAST's build among the slowest of the non-learned structures it tested.

When a learned index or hash table fits. In the same SOSD table, RMI (180.90 ns, 48 MB), RadixSpline (266.58 ns, 4 MB) and PGM (326.48 ns, 14 MB) are all faster and smaller than FAST (435.33 ns, 102 MB). If order does not matter, the hash tables took 94-115 ns.

CPUs without AVX-512F, non-x86 targets, or binaries that must be portable. Without AVX-512F you get an unbenchmarked scalar C fallback (a linear scan with early exit), and build.rs ties the binary to the build machine's CPU.
When you need exact-match or membership answers, duplicate keys, arbitrary payload types, range iteration, or more than about 2.1 billion u64 keys (see gotchas).
Proprietary or closed-source distribution (GPL-3.0), or when you need a maintained dependency: it has no README, no docs, no releases and no activity since April 2020.

integration.form: crate (Cargo lib + staticlib with a C-ABI header fast64.h; git-only, not published on crates.io)
integration.dependencies: num 0.2 (Rust); cc build-dependency plus a C compiler for c/lookup.c; criterion and rand for dev only. SOSD builds it with `cargo build --release` and links target/release/libfast64.a.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2018 edition with a C compiler that accepts -march=native (GCC or Clang). MSRV not documented, and Cargo.lock is gitignored, so dependency versions float. SOSD's README targets Ubuntu 20.04 with clang and rustup stable.
integration.platforms: x86-64. The AVX-512F SIMD path is chosen when build.rs detects avx512f on the build host (CPUID). Other x86-64 CPUs get a scalar C fallback. Non-x86 is not documented: build.rs uses an x86-only feature check. Windows/MSVC is not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Lookups only read (&self, no interior mutability), and SOSD ran 40 concurrent threads through the C API. But the Rust FAST<T> struct holds raw pointers (Vec<*const T>), so it is neither Send nor Sync, and sharing it across Rust threads needs an unsafe wrapper.

gotchas: The SIMD path is picked at build time. build.rs checks avx512f on the machine running cargo and compiles lookup.c with -march=native. A binary built on an AVX-512 host can fault on a CPU without it, and cross-compiling picks the host's path, not the target's.

It returns bounds, not matches. A query below the minimum key returns (0, min_val); a query at or above the maximum returns (max_val, T::MAX). Keys must already be sorted ascending (min and max are taken from the first and last element, and order is never checked). Duplicate-key behavior is not documented, and SOSD only runs the 64-bit wrapper on unique-key datasets.

Unsafe memory handling. copy_to_aligned passes a 128-byte-aligned allocation to Vec, which frees it with T's smaller alignment; the source comment admits this, and it breaks Rust's allocator contract. Empty input or unequal key/value lengths panic (unwrap/assert_eq), and the C API has no error return. The build copies the input three times and allocates a small Vec per page, which helps explain the slow build.

Child offsets are stored through `index as u32`, so a u64 tree whose leaf layer exceeds 2^32 slots (about 2^31 keys) silently truncates offsets. The bundled Criterion bench imports a nonexistent `fast64::Fast64` type and does not compile as shipped. fast64.h uses a bare extern "C" block and includes no <stdint.h>, so it only works from C++.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: RMI, RadixSpline and PGM-index all beat it on both latency and size in the same SOSD table, and ALEX, LIPP and HOT also accept inserts, so pick FAST only if you want a model-free comparison tree on AVX-512 hardware (nothing to tune except the sampling rate, and depth depends on key count, not key distribution). Its SOSD strengths are highly concurrent or fence-separated lookups: it scaled 32x at 40 threads and barely moved with fences that slowed RMI and RS by about 50%, though the learned indexes still had the better size/latency trade-off.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Xeon Gold 6230, the SOSD paper (Marcus et al., PVLDB 14(1)) ran 10M random lookups on a 32-bit version of the 200M-key amzn dataset: the fastest FAST variant took 435.33 ns per lookup at 102 MB, including last-mile binary search (its size matches a tree sampling every 16th key), against 482.11 ns at 166 MB for the fastest STX B-Tree variant, about 1.1x faster. No compiler or version is stated (SOSD's CMake uses -march=native -ffast-math, and build.rs compiles the C kernel with -march=native), and the 32x figure compares FAST at 40 threads with FAST at one thread, not with B-Tree.
status_note: Abandoned after 12 commits over 10 days (last 2020-04-23), with no README, releases or crates.io package and two outside Oct 2025 PRs (a C++23/Highway port and CI) closed unmerged; at about 500 lines of Rust and 150 of C it is easy to vendor, but GPL-3.0 copyleft applies and you would maintain it yourself.
